edge_cases.scenario: Consumer mails a CRA dispute with attached proof (cancelled check showing the account was paid, or a police report for an identity-theft account). The CRA converts it into an e-OSCAR ACDV containing only a two-digit dispute code and a short free-text line, never transmitting the documents; the furnisher re-checks its internal records, sees the same balance, and verifies.
edge_cases.gap_description: Checklist item 5 makes 'whether the furnisher reviewed the supporting documents the consumer submitted' dispositive, but in the overwhelming majority of real disputes the CRA never forwards those documents. Applied as encoded, the node tells the consumer the furnisher plainly violated § 1681s-2(b), when the furnisher's duty is measured by 'all relevant information provided by the CRA' — and the real target may be the CRA's § 1681i(a)(2) failure to forward the substance of the dispute and its documentation. The node neither flags the ACDV-truncation problem nor preserves the parallel CRA claim.

edge_cases.scenario: Consumer disputes a collection account in writing directly with the debt collector, which continues reporting the tradeline to the bureaus without any 'disputed by consumer' notation; the consumer never filed a bureau dispute and asks what remedy she has.
edge_cases.gap_description: The practical_enforcement_note tells the consumer that a direct dispute carries no private remedy and she must route through a CRA. That is right as to FCRA § 1681s-2(a)(8) but materially misleading where the furnisher is a debt collector: FDCPA § 1692e(8) independently and privately prohibits communicating known-disputed debt information without disclosing the dispute, and it is triggered by a direct dispute. The node cross-references only § 1692g validation, so a consumer with a live § 1692e(8) claim would be told she has none.

edge_cases.scenario: Consumer pulls her own report through a monitoring app, disputes an inaccurate late-payment notation, the furnisher does a token verification, and the error stays. No lender ever pulled the report, she was never denied credit, and she has no out-of-pocket loss; she sues in federal court seeking statutory and punitive damages for a willful violation.
edge_cases.gap_description: The remedies note states that willfulness opens statutory damages 'without proof of actual loss,' which post-TransUnion v. Ramirez is not sufficient for Article III standing: absent dissemination of the inaccurate information to a third party (or some other concrete harm), a federal-court claim is dismissed for lack of standing no matter how willful. The node's checklist asks about damages and willfulness but never about whether the inaccurate report was actually published to anyone, so a consumer with a self-pull-only dispute is told she has a viable statutory-damages claim when she likely cannot get into federal court at all.

results.derivation_summary: Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2), a debt collector is presumed to comply with the FDCPA's harassment-by-repeated-calls prohibition (§ 1692d(5)) if it places no more than seven calls to a particular person about a particular debt within seven consecutive days, and does not call that person about that debt within the seven consecutive days following a telephone conversation about it (the conversation date counts as day one). Exceeding either limit flips the presumption: the collector is presumed to violate § 1006.14(b)(1) and FDCPA § 806(5). Calls placed with the person's prior consent given directly to the collector (within seven days of that consent), calls not connected to the dialed number, and calls to the third parties listed in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii)-(vi) do not count toward the frequencies, and 'particular debt' means each separate debt in collection, except that student loan debts serviced under a single account number when obtained count as one debt. Note that state law may be stricter — 940 CMR 7.04(1)(f) limits collectors to two telephone communications per debt in each seven-day period to a debtor's personal number.

results.derivation_summary: Section 1692e bars a debt collector from using any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with collecting a debt, and then lists sixteen specific violations — including falsely implying government affiliation or bonding (1); misstating the character, amount, or legal status of a debt or the collector's lawful fees/services (2); posing as an attorney (3); threatening arrest, seizure, garnishment, attachment, or sale that is unlawful or not actually intended (4); threatening any action that cannot legally be taken or is not intended (5); falsely implying that transfer of the debt strips the consumer of defenses (6); implying the consumer committed a crime (7); communicating credit information known to be false or failing to note a debt is disputed (8); using documents simulating court or government process or that are falsely implied to be, or not to be, legal process (9), (13), (15); using false or deceptive means to collect or to obtain consumer information (10); failing to give the 'mini-Miranda' disclosures (11); falsely claiming accounts were sold to innocent purchasers for value (12); using a business name other than the collector's true name (14); and falsely implying the collector is or works for a consumer reporting agency (16). The §1692e(11) disclosure duty is now operationalized by 12 C.F.R. § 1006.18(e): disclose in the initial communication that the collector is attempting to collect a debt and that information obtained will be used for that purpose (repeated in the initial written communication if the first contact was oral), disclose debt-collector status in every later communication, with an exception for formal pleadings in a legal action. Judicial gloss adds that the misstatement must be material — capable of influencing the consumer's decision or action regarding the debt — measured under either the least sophisticated consumer or reasonable consumer standard depending on the circuit; and multiple circuits treat suing or threatening suit on a known time-barred debt (and, in some circuits, dunning letters implying a stale debt is enforceable) as violating §§ 1692e(2)(A), (5), and/or (10). These prohibitions apply only to a 'debt collector' as defined in § 1692a(6) (subject to the § 1692a(6)(F) carve-outs for fiduciary/escrow-incidental activity, originated debts, debts not in default when obtained, and commercial secured-party debts) collecting a 'debt' as defined in § 1692a(5) (consumer obligations primarily for personal, family, or household purposes).

results.derivation_summary: A debt collector may not use any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with collecting a debt. results.derivation_summary: Under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a), unless the information is in the initial communication or the debt is already paid, a debt collector must, within five days of the initial communication, send a written notice stating: the amount of the debt; the name of the creditor owed; that the debt will be assumed valid unless the consumer disputes it within 30 days of receipt of the notice; that if the consumer disputes it in writing within that 30-day period the collector will obtain and mail verification of the debt or a copy of a judgment; and that on written request within the 30-day period the collector will give the name and address of the original creditor. Regulation F (12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(a)(1), (c)) allows the validation information to be given orally in the initial communication or by a validation notice in or within five days of that communication. The dispute window ('validation period') runs from the date the collector provides the validation information and ends 30 days after the consumer receives — or is assumed to receive — it; the collector may assume receipt on any date at least five days (excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays, and Sundays) after it provides the information (§ 1006.34(b)(5)). If an original notice is undeliverable and a subsequent notice is sent, the end date is recalculated from actual or assumed receipt of the subsequent notice (comment 34(b)(5)-2). A user who converts a semimonthly figure to weekly by dividing by 2.167, or who doubles the 48x floor to 96x for a semimonthly period, gets a materially wrong exempt-earnings floor (96x vs. 104x) and an overstated garnishment. Pay period is in fact dispositive to any dollar result.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor already has 25% of his wages withheld under an existing child-support income withholding order. A judgment creditor on an old medical/credit-card debt then serves an earnings withholding order, and the debtor asks how much more can lawfully be taken.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats the 20%/40% cap as the standalone maximum for the consumer creditor and states 'anything withheld beyond that is unlawful,' with no priority or aggregation rule. Under CCP §§ 706.023, 706.031 and 706.052, support withholding has absolute priority and the consumer EWO is satisfied only out of what remains within the overall cap — often producing zero for the consumer creditor. Applying the encoded rule tells the debtor an additional 20% can be taken when in reality little or nothing can be, and conversely fails to flag that an employer withholding both is over-withholding.

edge_cases.scenario: A single parent earning about $950/week in disposable earnings in Los Angeles is subject to a consumer-debt garnishment and cannot cover rent and food after the withholding. She asks how much the creditor can take.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node presents the 20%/40% formula as the complete determination of lawful withholding and omits the financial-hardship claim of exemption under CCP § 706.051(b)/706.105, which lets a judgment debtor obtain a reduction to zero for earnings necessary for the support of the debtor and dependents (for non-necessaries consumer judgments). For a large share of low- and moderate-wage garnishment targets — the typical user of this rule — answering 'the creditor may take X' without the exemption pathway is materially misleading about the actual amount they will end up paying and about the procedural step they must take within the 10-day window.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor who moved to California 18 months ago and bought a home with $500,000 of equity files a Chapter 7 bankruptcy and wants to know how much of the home she can keep from creditors. Her county's median price yields a formula exemption well above $500,000.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node ignores the bankruptcy overlay: 11 U.S.C. § 522(p) caps the homestead exemption (currently ~$190,000) for equity acquired within 1,215 days before filing, § 522(o) reduces it for equity from fraudulent conversion, § 522(b)(3)(A)'s 730-day domicile rule can force use of another state's (or federal) exemptions, and California debtors may alternatively elect the CCP § 703.140(b) 'wildcard' scheme with a much smaller homestead figure. A debtor told she has a $600,000-plus exemption could lose the house. Most real homestead-exemption questions arise in bankruptcy, and none of these limits appear in the logic or checklist.

edge_cases.scenario: A homeowner asks whether her equity is safe where the claimant is an IRS tax lien, a recorded child-support arrears judgment, a mechanic's lien from a contractor who remodeled the house, or an HOA assessment lien — not a garden-variety tort or credit-card judgment.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist lists no dispositive fact about the nature of the debt or lien, so the node computes a large exemption and reports protection. But the CCP § 704.710 exemption is inapplicable or subordinated as to federal tax liens (preempted), consensual deeds of trust, mechanic's liens, and is expressly limited against support judgments (CCP § 703.070, § 704.720 proceeds orders). These are common creditor types and the answer flips entirely.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment creditor records an abstract of judgment against a debtor whose home has only $150,000 of equity, far under the exemption. The debtor is told the equity is 'protected,' then tries to sell or refinance and escrow demands payoff of the judgment lien.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node conflates exemption from forced sale with lien avoidance. An abstract of judgment attaches to an automatic (undeclared) homestead in full and must be paid or avoided on a voluntary sale; only where a homestead declaration has been recorded does CCP § 704.950 limit attachment to surplus over the exemption, and voluntary-sale proceeds are exempt only six months under § 704.720(b) if reinvested. The declared-vs-automatic distinction and the proceeds rule are absent from both the logic and the checklist, yet they determine the practical outcome.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment debtor voluntarily sold her car to a private buyer for $9,000 two weeks ago and deposited the cash in her checking account; the judgment creditor then levied the bank account. She asks whether $7,500 of that money is protected as her vehicle exemption.
edge_cases.gap_description: The rule's 'applies_to' language sweeps in 'execution-sale proceeds, or insurance/indemnification proceeds,' and the checklist asks only for the date proceeds were received, never whether the sale was an execution sale or a voluntary private sale. CCP § 704.010(b) protects only proceeds of an execution sale or insurance/indemnification proceeds — proceeds of a voluntary sale are not covered by this exemption at all. A debtor told $7,500 in her bank account is protected would be materially misinformed and could lose the levy fight (she would need a different theory, e.g. tracing to exempt funds or § 703.140(b) in bankruptcy).

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor with a car worth $12,000 subject to a $3,000 auto loan is facing repossession by the auto lender itself (or a mechanic's lien foreclosure by the shop holding the car), and asks whether the $7,500 exemption protects his equity.
edge_cases.gap_description: Neither the logic nor the checklist asks what kind of creditor/process is involved. CCP § 704 exemptions apply to enforcement of money judgments by levy; they do not defeat a consensual security interest (purchase-money auto lien) or a statutory lien foreclosure, and § 703.010 limits exemptions to enforcement-of-judgment proceedings. Applying the node as encoded tells a debtor his $7,500 of equity is 'protected from levy' when the repossessing secured lender can take the car regardless, which is the exact outcome he is asking about.

edge_cases.scenario: A married couple, both named as judgment debtors on a joint credit-card judgment, own two community-property vehicles with roughly $6,000 of equity each and want to know whether they can each claim $7,500 to shield both cars.
edge_cases.gap_description: The rule frames the exemption as aggregate 'across a debtor's motor vehicles' but never addresses multiple debtors/spouses or CCP § 703.110's treatment of marital and community property. California § 704 exemptions are generally not doubled by spouses, so the couple likely has one $7,500 exemption to allocate across both community-property vehicles, not $15,000. A married couple applying the node per-spouse would wrongly conclude both cars are fully protected and could fail to claim/allocate correctly, exposing roughly $4,500 of equity.

Telling this debtor the account is fair game is affirmatively wrong and would cause her to forgo the exemption claim / bank-review remedy. edge_cases.scenario: A debtor moved from Illinois to Houston 14 months ago, bought a $500,000 home outright with sale proceeds from her prior residence, and now wants to file Chapter 7 in Texas. She asks how much of her home equity is protected.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node addresses 11 U.S.C. § 522(p)'s 1,215-day equity cap but omits § 522(b)(3)(A)'s 730-day domicile rule, which is logically prior and often more dispositive. A debtor domiciled in Texas for less than 730 days before filing generally cannot use Texas exemptions at all and must use the prior state's (or the federal set), which can be dramatically smaller (Illinois: $15,000). Applying this node, she would be told she is protected up to ~$214,000 when her actual protection may be $15,000 or ~$31,575 federal — a materially wrong answer in exactly the 'recently relocated' scenario the node itself flags.

edge_cases.scenario: A creditor abstracted a judgment against the debtor in 2019 and recorded it in Travis County while the debtor was living in an apartment and renting out the house he owned there. In 2022 the debtor moved into that house as his residence; the creditor now seeks to foreclose the judgment lien.
edge_cases.gap_description: Neither the logic nor the checklist accounts for lien-timing: a judgment lien that validly attached before the property acquired homestead character is not defeated by later homestead impression, and non-homestead-at-the-time liens fall outside the § 41.001(b) exception list the node treats as exhaustive. The node would tell this debtor an ordinary judgment creditor categorically cannot reach his homestead, which is wrong here. The same omission also misses the related practical point that even a non-attaching abstract clouds title on sale absent a § 52.0012 release.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor took a two-year job assignment in Oklahoma, leased out her Dallas house to tenants, kept her Texas driver's license and homestead tax exemption, and intends to return. A judgment creditor is trying to execute on the Dallas house.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist makes 'whether the property is the debtor's actual residence' dispositive with no treatment of Texas abandonment doctrine, under which homestead character survives temporary absence — including renting the property out — absent clear intent to abandon and acquisition of a new homestead. Applied mechanically, the node would tell a temporarily absent or landlord-debtor that her property is not protected, which is wrong and could cause her to concede a claim she would win. Military deployment, job transfers, and eldercare relocations make this common.

The node's cap-driven framing ('are you under $50,000/$100,000?') will tell a debtor his bank and brokerage accounts are exempt when they are fully seizable — the single most common real-world Texas collection scenario.

It omits that federal-law collection mechanisms — administrative wage garnishment for defaulted federal student loans (20 U.S.C. § 1095a), IRS wage levy (26 U.S.C. § 6334), and court-ordered spousal maintenance — override the Texas wage exemption. edge_cases.scenario: A family that moved from California to Texas 14 months ago files Chapter 7 bankruptcy and asks whether their $85,000 of household goods, vehicles, and tools of trade is protected under the Texas $100,000 family cap.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no domicile/forum trigger. Under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A), a bankruptcy debtor domiciled in Texas for less than 730 days must use the exemptions of the prior state (or the federal set), so a recent Texas transplant filing bankruptcy gets nothing like the Texas $100,000 cap. Given Texas's very high in-migration and the frequency of bankruptcy as the context for exemption questions, applying the node as encoded would materially overstate protection for a common class of users.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer is handed the citation and petition by a process server on Monday, March 3, for a $4,200 credit-card debt in JP court. Using the node's 'computed from date of service,' she counts March 3 as day 1 and calculates her answer is due March 16; she files on March 17 believing she is one day early, but the court has already entered a default because it counted the 14 days differently.
edge_cases.gap_description: The rule states the deadline runs 'from date of service' but never encodes the computation convention in TRCP 500.5(a) (the day of service is excluded; the answer is due by the end of the 14th day after the day of service). An off-by-one error here is the single most consequential failure mode for this node, since it produces a default judgment. The checklist captures the service date but not the counting rule that turns it into a date.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues a consumer for $9,800 on a charged-off account, but files in a Texas county court at law rather than the justice court. The consumer is served, sees the amount is under $20,000, and is told the answer is due in 14 days, when in county court the answer is actually due at 10:00 a.m. on the Monday next after the expiration of 20 days from service.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist uses 'amount claimed is $20,000 or less' as a proxy for justice-court jurisdiction, but Texas county courts at law and district courts have concurrent jurisdiction over small debt claims and debt buyers routinely file there. The dispositive fact is which court issued the citation, not the amount. Applying the 14-day JP rule to a county-court citation gives a materially wrong deadline (and can make a defendant wrongly believe she has already defaulted, or misstate the Monday-next-after-20-days mechanic).

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer learns of a JP-court debt suit only when her bank account is frozen; the citation was left with a relative at an old address under a substituted-service order and she never personally received it. She asks how long she has to answer.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's checklist treats 'date of service' as an available, dispositive input and returns a flat 14-day deadline, which for a post-default defendant is misleading: the operative deadlines are a motion for new trial under TRCP 505.3 (within 14 days of the judgment) or a restricted appeal/bill of review, and defective or substituted service changes what 'date of service' even means. Default judgments after questionable service are extremely common in Texas debt collection, so a large share of real users hit this path and would be told their only relevant clock has run out.
